The news coverage I could check suggests the rain recorded during the spill fell mostly on 14–15 November, after the 17:14 start on Friday 13 November. **Questions I could check**

1. **When the event rain fell.** A Press Association weather report, published by the Falmouth Packet, said temperatures on Friday night (13 Nov) fell to −6.6°C in parts of the UK. It said that from Saturday (14 Nov) "heavy rain and showers are set to move in from the west and bring patchy rain… across the north and far west." It said Sunday (15 Nov) would bring "outbreaks of rain, some heavy." https://www.falmouthpacket.co.uk/news/national/26729224.freezing-temperatures-ease-milder-weather-showers-forecast/
   - This is a national forecast, not measured rain for this catchment. It fits the gauges' 10.8–12.25 mm falling well after the start, but it doesn't settle that.
2. **Pump failure, power cut or emergency discharge.** I searched for Devoran, Carnon Downs and Bissoe in a window around the spill and found nothing usable.
3. **Pollution reports for the Carnon River, 13–15 Nov.** I found nothing.
4. **Groundwater (the skeptic's infiltration idea).** A BBC report carried on Yahoo says regulators warned South West Water about "ongoing drought conditions." It says parts of Cornwall are "affected by severe drought" and reservoirs are only "starting to recover." https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/articles/water-supplies-risk-due-leaks-100732884.html
   - That points to low groundwater, which makes infiltration less likely. The article's exact date isn't shown; the page around it suggests mid-November 2026.
5. **Snowmelt.** The PA report mentions possible snow only in north-west Scotland (same Falmouth Packet link). Snowmelt in Cornwall looks unlikely.
6. **Spill history.** Cornwall Live lists the Carnon River among waters South West Water discharged sewage into after Storm Bert, a rain-driven event. https://www.cornwalllive.com/news/cornwall-news/sewage-released-cornwall-rivers-streams-9743328
   - I only saw the search snippet, not the full article. It doesn't name SBB00211, so it says nothing about dry-weather spills there.

**Left out:**
- **ITV West Country forecast page:** a snippet said "a bit of rain is expected during the evening across the Scillies and West Cornwall." That could support the skeptic, but the page is a rolling forecast and I can't confirm the snippet was about 13 November.
- **Met Office blog:** its snippet said Friday would begin "cold and frosty" with "plenty of sunshine" away from northern showers. When I opened the page, the text was cut off before that part, so I couldn't confirm which Friday it meant.
- Also dropped: copycat articles about South West Water's fines and dry-weather spills, a surf forecast, a weather forum, a LinkedIn profile, a US weather station's forecasts, and pages about the river's old mining pollution.

- **Points towards a breach:**
  - The three gauges agree there was almost no rain before the start (0.2 mm at most).

  - Hourly or radar rain for 16:00–18:00 on 13 Nov over the catchment.
  - Whether the spill has ended and when.
  - The permit conditions and the overflow's spill history.
  - Any South West Water or Environment Agency incident record.

The main unresolved alternative is a local shower over the catchment that the gauges missed. This is a credible dry-weather spill candidate, not a confirmed breach.

- **Timing of the event rain:** a Press Association report (Falmouth Packet) says heavy rain and showers were to "move in from the west" from Saturday 14 November, with "outbreaks of rain, some heavy" on Sunday 15 November. This is a national forecast, not measured catchment rainfall.

2. **Drought and groundwater.** BBC report carried by Yahoo:
   - Regulators warned South West Water about "ongoing drought conditions."

   - https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/articles/water-supplies-risk-due-leaks-100732884.html

3. **Earlier spills to the Carnon River.** Cornwall Live lists the Carnon River among waters that received South West Water sewage discharges after Storm Bert, a rain-driven event.

- Pump failure or power cut reports for Devoran, Carnon Downs or Bissoe

evidence.report:
**Findings: SBB00203 (South West Water), Plymouth Sound, 13–14 Nov 2026**

I found no source that reports this event, and none that supports or rules out an innocent cause on 13–14 November. The local reporting I found is about two different episodes in Plymouth in September and October 2026. One shows that tides can trigger overflows here without any rain. The other shows that the Environment Agency has recently found an unpermitted storm-overflow discharge nearby.

**Searches (5 searches, 2 page reads)**
1. South West Water overflow in Plymouth Sound, 10–20 Nov 2026: nothing about this event.
2. Plymouth weather on 13 Nov 2026: nothing usable. The only results were a syndicated national forecast giving a 12°C high in Plymouth on Saturday 14 Nov, with no rainfall figures for the site.
3. Plymouth pump station failure or power cut, Nov 2026: nothing usable. Results were about other places or were personal profiles.
4. "SBB00203" Plymouth: no source matches this code to a named overflow. It turned up the two earlier episodes below.
5. Plymouth Hoe sewage, spring tide or overflow, 12–18 Nov 2026: nothing usable. Results were US coastal flood notices and LinkedIn profiles.

**What supports a breach**
- On 2 October 2026 the Environment Agency said it had found "operational issues" at South West Water's treatment works on the River Plym. These included "what we consider to be an unpermitted discharge of sewage from storm overflow." It advised against bathing at Plymouth Hoe East and West, said the company "must address these issues as a matter of urgency," and said it would keep the matter under investigation. South West Water said it was investigating. (https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cvgl7ll8121yo)
- On 29 September 2026 South West Water was fined more than £7.8 million after pleading guilty to 18 charges. These were 17 illegal water discharge offences and one for failing to take reasonable remedial measures after a pumping station failure, between January 2015 and July 2021. Plymouth was one of the places involved. (https://www.plymouthherald.co.uk/news/plymouth-news/two-sewage-overflows-plymouth-active-11176653)
- Caveat: none of these sources names SBB00203. They show a recent pattern of non-compliance in this area, not a breach at this overflow.

**What supports an innocent explanation**
- Tides really can cause dry-weather triggers here. On 29 September 2026 a high spring tide set off the Oreston Quay and Marsh Mills storm overflows on the River Plym, with no rain mentioned:
  - At Oreston Quay, South West Water said spring tides get into the sewer and cause "a very diluted short spill when the tide drains out." The map logged it at about 8am, lasting 1 hour 40 minutes. The company said it was considering lining the sewers to stop tidal flooding.
  - At Marsh Mills, the company said the tide set off the alarm and "there is no evidence of a discharge taking place." That is a monitor activation with no actual spill. (Same Herald URL as above.)
- This supports the skeptic's tidal ingress and false-alarm explanations. But I found no evidence that the night of 13–14 November had a spring tide or surge, and an 8.6-hour event is much longer than the tide-linked events reported in September.

**Still unknown**
- Why and since when the monitor was offline, and whether the start and end times are real: no source found.
- Whether South West Water confirmed the event or gave a cause on its live overflow map: nothing found.
- Local rain that the gauges 5.5–5.9 km away might have missed: no source either way.
- Tide height or surge on 13–14 Nov: not found.
- Pump failures, blockages, power cuts or maintenance on 13–14 Nov: none reported in what I found.
- Permit conditions for SBB00203, its spill history, and groundwater effects in this catchment: not found.
- Any pollution report or bathing-water notice for 13–14 Nov: none found.

**Assessment**
The rain gauge data alone suggest a dry spill, and the Environment Agency's October finding nearby is relevant background. On the other hand, the monitor was offline and this estuarine area has a documented history of tide-triggered and false activations, so a non-rain trigger is plausible and the event may not be a real discharge. On the evidence found, the skeptic's low breach confidence (0.18) is reasonable.

To move the case forward, get:
- the tide tables for Plymouth (Devonport) for 13–14 November
- South West Water's own log for SBB00203, with the reason the monitor was offline
- the permit for this overflow from the Environment Agency's public register

# Evidence pack: NWL01051(2), Northumbrian Water, River Tees Estuary (spill started 14 Nov 2026, 07:34 UTC)

**Bottom line:** the sources I found back up the gauge: it was dry before and on the morning of the spill. I found no rain, snow or melt, and no reported incident or company statement. A dry-weather spill is still a reasonable working idea, but this is not proof of a breach. The pump-failure and tide explanations were never tested.

## Weather (checking the gauge and the skeptic's rain and snowmelt ideas)
- **13 Nov (Friday):** Durham, Darlington and Teesside had a chilly, sunny start, reaching about 7°C. Clear spells overnight were expected to bring frost, with temperatures at freezing by 9pm. https://www.thenorthernecho.co.uk/news/26726689.north-east-temperatures-plunge-0-weekend-begins/
- **14 Nov (Saturday, the spill day):** the same article forecast the day as "largely dry" with cloud and sunny intervals, highs around 8°C. It expected Middlesbrough to be similar, with rain only possibly reaching "some north-western areas" later in the day. Same URL.
  - This is a forecast written before the day, not a record of what happened.
  - The page says it was written by staff at USA Today, a partner paper, so treat it with some caution.
- **15 Nov (Sunday):** rain was expected across parts of County Durham and Teesside. That is after the spill started. Same URL.
- **Cold and snow:** Teesside Live (14 Nov) reported a yellow cold-health alert from 9pm on 15 Nov to 9am on 19 Nov. Snow was forecast for "next week", from Monday 16 Nov onwards. https://www.gazettelive.co.uk/news/teesside-news/cold-health-alert-issued-teesside-34912205
  - Both sources put cold weather and snow risk after the spill began, and neither reports earlier snow on Teesside. Snowmelt therefore has no support.

## Operational incidents, company or EA statements, tides
- A search for news about a Northumbrian Water spill or overflow on the Tees near Stockton or Thornaby in November 2026 found nothing usable.
- A search for a Teesside pumping-station failure or power cut on 14 Nov 2026 found nothing usable.
- A search for a Tees tidal surge or high tide on 14 Nov found nothing usable. The only tide pages returned were for other coasts.

## Site-specific data
- A search for NWL01051 found nothing about this overflow's permit or spill history.
- Northumbrian Water's own live overflow data feed is updated every 10 minutes. It is the place to check whether this event has ended or changed status. https://www.streamwaterdata.co.uk/datasets/nwg::northumbrian-water-storm-overflow-activity/about

## Findings

**What supports a breach**
- Independent weather reporting agrees with gauge 033108NE: sunny and dry on 13 Nov, and forecast largely dry on Teesside on 14 Nov (Northern Echo).
- Nothing points to snow or melt before the spill. Cold weather and snow were forecast only from 15–16 Nov onwards (Northern Echo, Teesside Live).
- Unrecorded heavy rain is unlikely. The press reports describe dry, cold weather, not localised storms.

**What supports an innocent explanation**
- I found nothing that confirms one. A frost overnight from 13 to 14 Nov is reported, but no source links frost or freezing to sewer problems.

**What is unknown**
- Whether a pump failed, the power went out or a sewer was blocked upstream. No reports were found, but that does not mean none happened. This is still the skeptic's strongest innocent explanation.
- Whether high tides or saltwater getting into the sewers in the Tees Estuary played a part. No tide data for the area was found.
- The permit conditions for this overflow, whether it counts as an emergency overflow, and its past spill record.
- Whether the spill has ended, and its status (currently null). Check the company's live feed above.
- Whether Northumbrian Water or the Environment Agency has issued any incident notice or statement. None was found.
- What actually happened on 14 Nov, as opposed to the forecast. Rainfall from other EA gauges and radar would settle whether it really was dry.

**Assessment:** the weather evidence makes a rain-driven spill less likely, which strengthens the "dry spill" case. The next steps are:
1. Get the company's live event record and the site's permit.
2. Get tide times for the Tees on 14 Nov.
3. Ask Northumbrian Water directly whether there was an operational incident.

evidence.report:
**Findings report: AWS00045 (Baldock pumping station, Norton Road), 14 November 2026**

**Bottom line:** I found nothing that confirms or rules out a breach. The rain gauges point to dry weather. But the monitor was offline and there's no outside record of a discharge, sewage on the ground or any reason for one. A breach finding isn't supported yet, and the question of whether the monitor was faulty still needs settling with Anglian Water's own data. I made 5 searches and read 2 pages in full.

**What the site is**
- A council-published copy of Anglian Water's overflow monitoring data lists AWS00045 as "BALDOCK PS · BALDOCK-NORTON ROAD SP", asset AWCLF10344. It's described as a "Storm discharge at pumping station" at grid reference TL2420034250, discharging to "Ivel (US Henlow) ONTO LAND". https://www.basildon.gov.uk/media/12899/Appendix-2-Anglian-Water-CSO-Monitoring-Data/pdf/Appendix_2_-_Anglian_Water_CSO_Monitoring_Data.pdf?m=1773832799050
- The same row has fields marked "Not Applicable" and values of "0:00:00" and "0". The extract doesn't say what those columns are or which year they cover, so I haven't drawn anything from them.

**What supports a breach**
- **Rain:** All three gauges show at most 0.2 mm before and during the event, from the feed's own data.
- **Weather reports:** A Guardian article from 14 November 2026 says it had been cold and frosty. It quotes the Met Office saying central and eastern England should stay dry with clear spells and some frost on the night of Saturday 14th. https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026/nov/14/uk-weather-milder-weekend-autumn-freeze-frost
  - This is a national report, not one about Baldock.
  - The dry forecast is for the night after the event ended (19:43 UTC on the 14th), so it only indirectly backs up the dry gauges.
  - It doesn't confirm conditions in Baldock during 01:36–19:43 UTC on 14 November.
- **Missed downpour:** I found no news or Met Office report of rain in the Baldock area on 13–14 November. That makes the skeptic's missed-shower idea less likely, but it doesn't disprove it.

**What supports an innocent explanation**
- **Offline monitor (the skeptic's main objection):** The feed itself marks the monitor offline and the status as null. I found no source that confirms or rules out a sensor or data fault.
- **Past pipe failures on Norton Road:** HertsLive reported that the sewer pipe on Norton Road burst on 17 August 2021, spilling onto the path at Ivel Springs Nature Reserve. Anglian Water blamed debris or an object in the pipe. https://www.hertfordshiremercury.co.uk/news/hertfordshire-news/burst-sewer-pipe-floods-baldock-5826062
  - The same article says the main sewer in the town burst more seriously on 27 April 2021. The Environment Agency rated it a category 2 groundwater incident.
  - Anglian Water said there was "a discharge onto the land" that was cleared up, and that it would fit pressure monitors on the main.
  - This shows equipment failures have happened at this location, so the skeptic's pump or main failure idea is believable in principle. But it's history from 2021, and there's no evidence of a failure in November 2026.

**What is unknown (no usable source found)**
- Whether anything actually discharged on 14 November 2026, or whether the monitor was faulty. I found no notes from Anglian Water and no coverage of the event.
- When the monitor went offline, or whether any monitoring fault or maintenance was reported.
- Whether there was a pump failure, power cut, blockage or burst main around 14 November. My search for Norton Road or Ivel Springs sewage incidents from October to December 2026 found nothing usable.
- The permit conditions for this site, such as pass-forward flow and storm tank requirements.
- Any Environment Agency or Ofwat investigation at this site, past dry-weather spills, or local complaints about sewage on land around 14 November 2026. The only Anglian Water news I found was about national Ofwat action, nothing specific to this site.

**Left out:** event listings, forecast widgets (including one for Waltham in the US), a satire site, LinkedIn profiles, content farms, and a FixMyStreet report about a different place. I also left out a North Herts Council agenda item about a different sewer (Ivy Lane), and the River Ivel group's own website, which isn't a news outlet or regulator.

Groundwater infiltration: no evidence of a rising water table, and there was no rain at all in the 48h before
objections_standing: EDM sensor fault or blip while the monitor was offline: the feed flags monitor_offline=true and status=null, and nothing confirms or rules out a fault
Data-feed or transmission error producing a spurious 18-hour record: unverified either way

Pump failure, power loss or burst main causing an emergency discharge: plausible in principle given the 2021 Norton Road failures, but such a discharge would still be a real, reportable pollution event rather than an innocent rainfall explanation
Localised shower missed by the gauges: weakened but not disproven, since three gauges agree and no rain was reported
ruling.reasoning: The rainfall evidence for dry conditions is strong. Three gauges within 7.7 km recorded at most 0.2 mm in the 24h before and during the event, and none recorded any rain 24-48h before. A national report describes cold, frosty, dry conditions. The fact-checker also found no local rain reports, which makes a missed downpour unlikely. The asset is a pumping station storm discharge onto land at Baldock, and there were real sewer failures nearby in 2021. That makes a genuine operational discharge believable, and a pump or main failure would still be worth investigating rather than excusing it. However, the dominant objection still stands: the monitor is flagged offline and the status is null. That directly undermines whether the 18.1-hour event reflects a real discharge at all, and no external evidence (Anglian Water notes, complaints, news) corroborates that one happened. The case merits a query to Anglian Water about the monitor's status, but the probability that this is a genuine dry-day spill is modest, slightly above the skeptic's 0.25 because the dry weather is well supported.

evidence.report:
I found nothing published that explains this spill innocently: no reported asset failure, no unexpected rain and no monitor-fault notice. One published source confirms the spill and gives an end time. A weather forecast supports the dry readings from the rain gauges. Most of the investigator's questions couldn't be answered from public sources. I used all 5 searches and 2 of 3 page reads.

## What the sources show

**1. The spill happened, and has since ended.**
- NWL00415 appears to be Northumbrian Water's **Dalton‑Le‑Dale CSO**, a storm overflow into Dawdon Dene Beck, in the Seaham Peterlee Coast catchment. https://www.floodmapper.co.uk/stations/dalton-le-dale-cso-dalton-le-dale/metric/bf40ffca-5ce5-408d-8641-649320a6455a
  - I matched it by name and river, not by the ID or coordinates, so the match should be confirmed.
- On the same page, the discharge **started 14 Nov 2026 at 6:26:20 PM**, the same time as our feed. It **ended 15 Nov 2026 at 11:01:21 AM**, about 995 minutes or 16.6 hours. It is the only event in the window shown.
  - That fills in our feed's missing end time and roughly matches its 16.4 hours.
- **Caveat:** FloodMapper is an independent site. It republishes data that the Environment Agency oversees and says it doesn't check that data. It is a reasonable copy of the company's monitor feed, but not an official record.

**2. The weather was dry.**
- The Northern Echo said Friday 13 Nov was chilly and sunny across County Durham, with frost forming overnight. It expected Saturday 14 Nov to stay "largely dry", with rain possible later only in north‑western areas. It said rain would arrive across parts of County Durham on Sunday 15 Nov. https://www.thenorthernecho.co.uk/news/26726689.north-east-temperatures-plunge-0-weekend-begins/
  - The page is labelled as written by sister title USA Today.
  - It is a **forecast published on 13 Nov, not measured rainfall**.
  - It doesn't say what time rain reached the Seaham coast on the 15th.

**3. No reported incident.**
- A search for blockages, pumping station failures or power cuts at Seaham, Dalton‑le‑Dale or Murton (7–25 Nov 2026) found **nothing**.
- A search for news of a sewage spill at Dawdon or Seaham in November 2026 also found **nothing**. Those results were about Dawdon's mine‑water scheme and bonus‑ban stories, which have nothing to do with this site.

## Findings

**Supports a breach**
- Published monitor data confirms a single continuous discharge of about 16.6 hours. It started at the time our feed gives, and there is no sign of a short sensor blip.
- The local paper expected 13–14 Nov to be dry and frosty across County Durham. Rain was only expected on the 15th, when the spill was already about 16 hours old. This matches the near‑zero readings at both gauges.
- I found no published pump failure, blockage or power cut that would explain an emergency discharge.

**Supports an innocent explanation**
- Nothing I found directly supports one.
- The Northern Echo forecast rain for parts of County Durham on 15 Nov. That could matter only for the last few hours before the 11:01 end, and both gauges recorded 0.0 mm during the spill.
- Missing news coverage doesn't prove there was no asset fault. Companies often don't publicise them.

**Unknown**
- The environmental permit and its conditions (pass‑forward flow, storm tank).
- The site's yearly spill counts and hours.
- Whether Northumbrian Water has flagged this event as a monitor error or an operational problem.
- Environment Agency incident reports or public complaints about this beck or coast.
- Tide, surge or groundwater effects. The outfall is near the coast, so this is still worth checking with the Environment Agency, but I found no evidence either way.
- Measured rainfall from radar or other gauges, as opposed to a forecast.
- Details of the company's earlier likely‑breach case.

**Overall:** the published evidence agrees with the dry‑spill flag and with the skeptic's 0.78 confidence. The most useful next step is to ask Northumbrian Water and the Environment Agency directly for the permit, any record of an asset fault or monitor error on 14–15 Nov, and tide and groundwater data.

- 14 Nov as expected to be "largely dry", with rain possible later only in north-western areas
- rain arriving in parts of County Durham on 15 Nov

**Caveats on the rainfall evidence:**
- The Northern Echo article is a forecast, not measured rainfall.
- The page is labelled as written by a sister title.
- It does not say when rain reached the Seaham coast on 15 Nov.
- The feed's "during" window appears to reflect a snapshot taken at 16.4 h. The last roughly 10 minutes before the 11:01 end may not be covered by the gauge figures.

## Innocent explanations considered

The skeptic's assessment, with the adjudicator's ruling:

| Explanation | Skeptic plausibility | Status |
|---|---|---|
| EDM sensor fault or short blip | Low | **Refuted.** FloodMapper shows a single continuous event of about 16.6 h. |
| Data-feed or timestamp error | Low | **Refuted.** The same start time appears in an independent source. |
| Localised rain missed by gauges | Low | **Largely refuted.** The gauge is 0.8 km away and the forecast was dry for 13–14 Nov. |
| Snowmelt | Low | **Refuted.** No evidence of snow before the event. |
| High groundwater or infiltration | Medium | **Standing, unverified.** Limited weight given the dry antecedent conditions. |
| Tidal backflow or surge (outfall near the coast) | Medium | **Standing, unverified.** No evidence either way. |
| Emergency discharge from pump failure, blockage or power loss | Medium | **Standing.** No public report found, but companies often do not publicise faults. A discharge like this would still be a dry-day discharge warranting investigation. |

**Skeptic's strongest objection (quoted):**

> "A 16.4-hour continuous overflow recorded by an online EDM monitor, with virtually zero rainfall at two gauges – the nearest only 0.8 km away – is inconsistent with a brief sensor glitch or missed rain, making a genuine dry-spill the most plausible explanation."

The skeptic's own strongest objection therefore favours a breach. Its confidence in a breach was 0.78.

**Strongest remaining case against a breach:** tidal or surge influence at a near-coastal outfall, or an unpublicised asset failure. Neither has been checked against data.

## Web evidence (cited)

1. **FloodMapper: Dalton-Le-Dale CSO live discharge page.** https://www.floodmapper.co.uk/stations/dalton-le-dale-cso-dalton-le-dale/metric/bf40ffca-5ce5-408d-8641-649320a6455a

   - Shows a discharge from 14 Nov 2026 18:26:20 to 15 Nov 2026 11:01:21, about 995 minutes.
   - This is the only event in the window shown.
   - It is an unofficial republication, and the site was matched by name only.
2. **The Northern Echo: "North East temperatures plunge to below 0 as the weekend begins".** https://www.thenorthernecho.co.uk/news/26726689.north-east-temperatures-plunge-0-weekend-begins/
   - Forecast published 13 Nov: 13–14 Nov dry and frosty across County Durham, rain from 15 Nov.

**Searches that found nothing:**
- Blockage, pumping station failure or power cut at Seaham, Dalton-le-Dale or Murton in November 2026.
- News of a sewage spill at Dawdon or Seaham in November 2026.

The absence of reports is not proof that no incident occurred.

## Confidence and recommendation

**Confidence: 0.80 (likely breach)**

What supports this:
- Near-zero rainfall across all windows at a gauge 0.8 km from the outfall.
- A continuous discharge of about 16.6 hours, independently corroborated.
- A dry forecast for the period.
- No published innocent explanation.

What creates residual uncertainty:
- The data source is unofficial.
- The site was matched to NWL00415 by name only.
- Tidal and groundwater effects have not been checked.
- Asset-fault records have not been seen.

**Severity:** high. The site has no prior cases in our records. Our internal records hold one other likely-breach case for Northumbrian Water at a different site. This is not a public finding.

**Recommendation:** Forward to the Environment Agency as a **possible** breach for investigation. Request:
1. Confirmation that NWL00415 is Dalton-le-Dale CSO, plus the official EDM record of the event.
2. The environmental permit conditions, including pass-forward flow and storm tank requirements.
3. Any operator record of an asset fault or monitor error on 14–15 Nov 2026.
4. Tide, surge and groundwater data for the outfall.
5. Annual EDM spill counts and hours for the site.

**Unknowns not resolved by public sources:**
- Permit conditions
- Annual returns
- Environment Agency incident reports or public complaints
- Radar-measured rainfall

evidence.report:
**Findings: overflow NWL00073 (Northumbrian Water) discharging to Demons Beck, event started 14 Nov 2026 at 23:10 UTC**

I used all 5 searches and 2 of the 3 fetches. No source I found mentions this overflow or Demons Beck by name. The useful sources were weather forecasts for the area and general pages about the company. I found no observed rainfall reports, incident reports, permit details or explanation from the company.

**1. Weather. The forecasts don't match the gauges (most important finding)**
- The Northern Echo forecast that Saturday 14 November would be "largely dry" in Darlington, Durham, Middlesbrough and Hartlepool. It also said "some north-western areas could see rain arriving later in the day." For Sunday 15 November it forecast "outbreaks of rain expected across parts of County Durham and Teesside." The night of 13–14 November was forecast to be freezing with frost. https://www.thenorthernecho.co.uk/news/26726689.north-east-temperatures-plunge-0-weekend-begins/
- A Met Office post dated 14 November, quoted in a national PA article run by the Darlington and Stockton Times, said: "A wet and chilly start for many on Sunday morning with spells of heavy rain for many." The article added that "rain will be more persistent for northern England." https://www.darlingtonandstocktontimes.co.uk/news/national/26730021.yellow-cold-health-alerts-come-force-parts-uk-amid-frosty-weather/
- **Why this matters:** the spill started late Saturday night and, at 11.6 hours, runs to about 10:45 UTC on Sunday 15 November. That is the morning when rain was forecast for the region. Both gauges (6.3 km and 9.6 km away) show 0.0 mm during the spill.
- **Caveat:** these are forecasts, not measurements, and the Met Office quote covers all of the UK. They do not prove rain fell at Demons Beck. But they are enough reason to question the "dry weather" label until the gauge data is shown to be complete and up to date.

**2. Pump failure, power cut or blockage**
- I found no report of one. The only Northumbrian Water operational incident in the results was a burst water main in Newcastle city centre, which is unrelated (https://www.dailyrecord.co.uk/news/uk-world-news/burst-water-main-causes-flooding-37877811).
- Finding nothing in the news is not proof nothing happened. The company's own incident records would settle it.

**3. Permit conditions**
- Northumbrian Water's own page says storm overflows discharge "during and after heavy rainfall conditions, with permission from the Environment Agency (EA)." https://www.nwl.co.uk/services/environmental-information/
- I did not find the permit number, pass-forward flow or storage terms for this overflow.

**4. Company enforcement history**
- BBC: Northumbrian Water agreed to pay £15.7m in a package set by Ofwat (the water regulator) after "failures in the maintenance and operations of its sewage and water network." I only saw the search snippet, not the full article. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cg4vpzpkqw2o
- I found nothing about Environment Agency enforcement for dry-weather spills at this site.

**5. Local reports and spill history**
- I found no public reports, photos or complaints about Demons Beck, and no annual spill records for this overflow.
- One lead I could not check: the search tool's summary said Northumbrian Water plans investment at "Aycliffe (Skerne)" for 2025–2030. The source snippet did not show this, so don't rely on it.

**What supports a breach**
- The gauge data from the feed: 0.0 mm during the spill, at most 0.2 mm in the 24 hours before, and 0.0 mm in the 24–48 hours before.
- The monitor is reported online, and the event has no recorded end time.
- Forecasts called for a dry Saturday locally, so the hours before the start were probably dry.
- I found no public report of a pump failure, power cut or blockage.
- The company has a recent Ofwat penalty for network maintenance and operation failures (BBC).

**What supports an innocent explanation**
- Rain was forecast for County Durham and Teesside on Sunday 15 November, including "heavy rain for many" on Sunday morning. That overlaps most of the spill. Local rain the two gauges missed, or gauge data not yet updated, is plausible. This makes the skeptic's "missed local rain" and "data/feed error" explanations stronger.
- A freezing night before the spill was forecast. That doesn't explain a discharge, but icing affecting the sensor can't be ruled out.

**What is unknown**
- Whether the spill has ended, and what end time the company's live feed now shows.
- Whether the gauge readings for "during" are complete, and what Environment Agency radar estimates or closer gauges show for the night of 14–15 November.
- Whether there was any pump, power or blockage incident.
- The permit terms for this overflow and whether any exemption applies.
- Groundwater and river levels for Demons Beck and the River Skerne.
- The overflow's spill history and any report to the Environment Agency about this event.

**Bottom line:** keep this as a candidate, not a likely breach, until rainfall for Sunday morning is confirmed from Environment Agency radar or closer gauges. If that shows no rain, the breach case gets much stronger.

# Evidence pack: possible dry-weather spill at NWL00073 (Demons Beck)

**Pipeline verdict:** needs_review | **Final confidence:** 0.4 (adjudicator) | **Skeptic confidence:** 0.3

## Summary

The live feed shows storm overflow NWL00073, operated by Northumbrian Water and discharging to Demons Beck, started an event at **2026-11-14 23:10:22 UTC**. The event had no recorded end time and had run **11.6 hours** when the data was captured. The two nearest Environment Agency rain gauges recorded **0.0 mm during the event**, at most **0.2 mm in the 24 hours before**, and **0.0 mm in the 24–48 hours before**. On these figures it looks like a dry-weather discharge.

However, regional forecasts predicted rain, possibly heavy, for County Durham and Teesside on the morning of Sunday 15 November. That period overlaps most of the event. Until observed rainfall for that window is confirmed, this is a **candidate for investigation, not a confirmed breach**.

## The spill (data)

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Site ID | NWL00073 |
| Company | Northumbrian Water |
| Receiving watercourse | Demons Beck |
| Location | 54.60584, -1.56452 |
| Event start | 2026-11-14 23:10:22 UTC |
| Event end | Not recorded (null) |
| Duration at data capture | 11.6 hours (to about 10:46 UTC, 15 Nov) |
| Monitor offline | false |
| Status field | null |
| Feed classification | dry_spill_candidate |

Two points are worth noting:
- The `status` field is null, so the feed does not confirm the overflow is currently discharging.
- Because the event is open-ended, the "during" rainfall window may only cover up to the time the data was captured.

## Rainfall context

**Gauge data from the feed:**

| Gauge | Distance | 24–48h before | 0–24h before | During |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 032822 | 6.3 km | 0.0 mm | 0.0 mm | 0.0 mm |
| 030377 | 9.6 km | 0.0 mm | 0.2 mm | 0.0 mm |
| **Max** | | **0.0 mm** | **0.2 mm** | **0.0 mm** |

**Forecasts (not observations):**
- **Saturday 14 November:** forecast "largely dry" for Darlington, Durham, Middlesbrough and Hartlepool. A frost was forecast for the night of 13–14 November. ([Northern Echo](https://www.thenorthernecho.co.uk/news/26726689.north-east-temperatures-plunge-0-weekend-begins/))
- **Sunday 15 November:** "outbreaks of rain expected across parts of County Durham and Teesside." ([Northern Echo](https://www.thenorthernecho.co.uk/news/26726689.north-east-temperatures-plunge-0-weekend-begins/))
- **Met Office post, quoted in a PA article:** "A wet and chilly start for many on Sunday morning with spells of heavy rain for many." The article added that "rain will be more persistent for northern England." The Met Office quote covers the whole UK. ([Darlington and Stockton Times](https://www.darlingtonandstocktontimes.co.uk/news/national/26730021.yellow-cold-health-alerts-come-force-parts-uk-amid-frosty-weather/))

**What this means:**
- The event started late on a forecast-dry Saturday night, so the start itself is plausibly dry.
- Most of the event falls in the Sunday-morning window when rain was forecast.
- The gauges show no rain in that window. This conflicts with the forecasts and needs checking against observed data, such as EA radar or closer gauges.

## Innocent explanations considered

**Skeptic's strongest objection, quoted in full:**
> "There is a credible risk that a sensor or data-feed error produced a false positive event signal, meaning the reported discharge may not have actually occurred."

| Explanation | Skeptic plausibility | Adjudicator view |
|---|---|---|
| Pump failure, power cut or blockage forcing an emergency discharge | High | **Standing.** Neither confirmed nor ruled out. It would still be a dry-weather discharge worth investigating, but may not be a permit breach. |
| Localised rain missed by the gauges (6.3 km and 9.6 km away) | Medium | **Standing, and strengthened** by forecasts of Sunday-morning rain. Gauge data may also be incomplete or delayed. |
| Data-feed or classification error | Medium | **Standing.** The forecast freezing night gives a small chance of sensor icing. |
| Transient sensor or monitor fault | Low | Considered together with the data-feed error above. |
| High groundwater or infiltration | Medium | **Refuted (weakly supported).** 0.0 mm in the 24–48h window, and a largely dry Saturday was forecast. |
| Snowmelt | Low | **Refuted.** Only frost was forecast, with no evidence of prior snow. |
| Tidal back-flow or river surge | Low | **Refuted.** Demons Beck is an inland tributary, not tidal. |

**Also unresolved:** the permit terms for this overflow and whether any exemption applies.

## Web evidence (cited)

- **Site-specific sources:** none found. No source found mentions NWL00073 or Demons Beck by name.
- **Weather:** see the Rainfall context section above ([Northern Echo](https://www.thenorthernecho.co.uk/news/26726689.north-east-temperatures-plunge-0-weekend-begins/); [Darlington and Stockton Times](https://www.darlingtonandstocktontimes.co.uk/news/national/26730021.yellow-cold-health-alerts-come-force-parts-uk-amid-frosty-weather/)).
- **Operational incidents:**
  - No public report was found of a pump failure, power cut or blockage at or near this site.
  - The only Northumbrian Water incident in the results was a burst water main in Newcastle, which is unrelated ([Daily Record](https://www.dailyrecord.co.uk/news/uk-world-news/burst-water-main-causes-flooding-37877811)).
  - Finding no news report does not mean no incident occurred.
- **Permit basis:**
  - Northumbrian Water's own page says storm overflows discharge "during and after heavy rainfall conditions, with permission from the Environment Agency (EA)" ([NWL](https://www.nwl.co.uk/services/environmental-information/)).
  - The permit number, pass-forward flow and storage terms for this overflow were not found.
- **Company enforcement history:**
  - Northumbrian Water agreed to pay £15.7m in an Ofwat enforcement package over "failures in the maintenance and operations of its sewage and water network." This is based on the search snippet only ([BBC](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cg4vpzpkqw2o)).
  - This is general context and is not specific to this site.
  - No EA enforcement history for dry spills at this site was found.
- **Public reports and spill history:** no public reports, photos or complaints about Demons Beck, and no annual spill records for this overflow, were found.

## Confidence and recommendation

**Confidence: moderate-low (0.4).**

**Supporting a breach:**
- Zero rainfall during the event at both gauges.
- Negligible rainfall in the 48 hours before.
- Monitor reported online.
- No recorded end time.
- No public report of an operational failure.

**Against a breach:**
- Regional forecasts predicted rain for most of the event window.
- A data or sensor error cannot be excluded.
- The permit terms are unknown.

**Recommendation for the reviewer:**
1. Before sending, check EA rainfall radar and any closer gauges for 23:00 UTC on 14 November to about 11:00 UTC on 15 November.
2. Check Northumbrian Water's live feed for the event's end time.
3. If observed rainfall was negligible, the case is substantially stronger and should be sent.
4. If significant rain is confirmed, consider closing the case or downgrading it.
5. If you cannot verify before sending, send the message below. It is framed as a possible breach for investigation.

## Draft message to the Environment Agency

> **Subject:** Report of a POSSIBLE storm overflow permit breach for investigation: NWL00073, Demons Beck (Northumbrian Water)
>
> Dear Environment Agency,
>
> I am writing to report a **possible** dry-weather discharge for your investigation. This is not a confirmed breach. I would be grateful if you could assess it.
>
> **Site:** Storm overflow NWL00073, Northumbrian Water, discharging to Demons Beck (54.60584, -1.56452).
>
> **Event:** The company's live storm overflow feed shows an event starting 2026-11-14 23:10:22 UTC. No end time was recorded, and the event had lasted 11.6 hours when the data was captured. The monitor was reported online.
>
> **Rainfall:** Environment Agency gauges 032822 (6.3 km) and 030377 (9.6 km) recorded 0.0 mm during the event, a maximum of 0.2 mm in the 24 hours before, and 0.0 mm in the 24–48 hours before.
>
> **Caveats:**
> - Regional forecasts predicted rain, possibly heavy, for County Durham and Teesside on the morning of 15 November. This overlaps most of the event. Localised rain the gauges did not record, or incomplete gauge data, is therefore possible.
> - A monitoring or data-feed error also cannot be ruled out.
> - I have found no public report of a pump failure, power cut or blockage, and I do not know this overflow's permit conditions.
>
> **Requests:** I would be grateful if you could:
> 1. Check radar and observed rainfall for the event window.
> 2. Confirm the event's duration with Northumbrian Water and establish whether any operational failure occurred.
> 3. Assess whether the discharge complied with the permit for this overflow.
>
> Kind regards,
> [Name]
> [Contact details]

# Evidence pack: TWL00049 (Thames Water, "Groundwater"), event from 15 Nov 2026 05:15 UTC

**Bottom line:** The evidence leans towards a breach but doesn't prove one. Bourton's overflow permit only allows spills caused by rainfall or snowmelt, and early-November reports point away from high groundwater. But I couldn't confirm that TWL00049 is the Bourton overflow, and I found no local data for 15 November itself.

## Can the site be identified?
- **Probably Bourton-on-the-Water (Cotswolds, River Windrush catchment), but not confirmed.** Thames Water's Groundwater Impacted System Management Plan for Bourton describes "a permitted land treatment area and overflow to the River Windrush" south of the village. Excess flow travels about 800 m to the land treatment area before reaching the river. The spill's coordinates are just south of Bourton, and a land treatment area could explain the "Groundwater" label. The plan never uses the ID TWL00049, though. https://www.bourtononthewater-pc.gov.uk/wp-content/uploads/sites/114/2025/07/bourton-on-the-water-groundwater-infiltration-mana_250713_233038.pdf
- The parish council confirms that Thames Water has produced this plan for Bourton. https://www.bourtononthewater-pc.gov.uk/the-council/emergency-planning/

## Investigator's questions
- **Permit condition:** The plan quotes the permit for the overflow to the land treatment area: "The discharge shall only occur when and only for as long as the flow passed forward is equal to or greater than the overflow setting indicated due to rainfall and/or snowmelt." Groundwater is not listed as an allowed cause. (Plan PDF above.)
- **Groundwater-impacted site?** Yes, Bourton is. The network is about 41 km, mostly separate foul sewers, serving 4,790 population equivalent. The plan says "in recent years" the foul system has been "overwhelmed for weeks or even months at a time" after prolonged heavy rain and raised groundwater. (Plan PDF.)
- **Previous dry-day spills:** The plan says the land treatment area has been used and "spill to river has occurred on both wet and dry days" when incoming flow exceeded capacity for long periods. It gives no dates or EDM figures. (Plan PDF.)
- **Groundwater in November 2026:** Water Magazine reported the EA's weekly report for 30 Oct–5 Nov. England was still in drought, with only 2 mm of rain that week after a wetter October (112% of average). River flows fell at all reporting sites, and groundwater "continued to fall at most monitoring sites" because dry soils limited recharge. This is a national summary from about 10 days before the spill, not a reading from a local borehole. https://www.watermagazine.co.uk/2026/11/09/drought-continues-to-grip-england-as-reservoir-levels-remain-below-average/

- **Rain radar, snowmelt, the EDM end time, whether Thames Water notified the EA, and local borehole levels:** I found nothing usable on any of these. My attempt to open the EA's report for 6–12 November failed because I had guessed the URL and it doesn't exist. The only source I found for later November was an aggregator site, which I've left out.

**What supports a breach**
- The permit, if this is the Bourton overflow, only allows spills caused by rainfall or snowmelt, not groundwater.
- The nearest gauge (1.1 km) recorded about 0 mm before and during the spill.
- England-wide in early November, groundwater was still falling and soils were dry. That weakens the "high groundwater" explanation, which the skeptic rated most plausible.
- Thames Water's own plan says dry-day spills at Bourton have happened before.
- No pump failure or other incident was reported.

**What supports an innocent explanation**
- Bourton is an officially recognised groundwater-impacted network that can be overwhelmed for weeks after wet spells. October 2026 was wetter than average nationally.
- The plan has a section on "anticipated unavoidable discharges". I didn't read that section in full, so I can't say what it covers.
- The 0.52 mm reading at the gauge 9.4 km away is small, but it shows there was some rain in the area during the event.

**Still unknown**
- Whether TWL00049 is the Bourton land-treatment overflow.
- Local groundwater and river levels on 15 November 2026.
- Rain radar for the area.
- Whether and when the event ended.
- Whether there was any operational fault, or any notification to the EA.

**Suggested next steps:** Match TWL00049 against Thames Water's EDM or permit register. Get EA borehole and Windrush river-level data for 13–15 November. Read the "anticipated unavoidable discharges" section of the plan.

# Evidence pack: TWL00049 (Thames Water), event starting 15 Nov 2026 05:15 UTC

**Pipeline verdict:** likely_breach (adjudicator confidence 0.68)

---

## Summary

Thames Water storm overflow **TWL00049** (receiving water recorded as "Groundwater", approx. 51.8699, -1.7455) logged a discharge starting **2026-11-15 05:15 UTC**. No end time was recorded, and the duration was **at least 5.6 hours** when the data was taken.

The nearest rain gauge (1.1 km) recorded **0.0 mm during the event** and **0.01 mm in each of the two 24-hour windows before it**. The event monitor was reported online.

The site is **probably, but not confirmed to be,** the Bourton-on-the-Water land-treatment overflow. Thames Water's published plan quotes that overflow's permit as allowing discharges only "due to rainfall and/or snowmelt".

The main uncertainties are:
- the site has not been confirmed as Bourton
- there is no local groundwater data for 15 November
- one section of Thames Water's plan, on "anticipated unavoidable discharges", has not been reviewed

---

## The spill (data)

|---|---|
| Site ID | TWL00049 |
| Company | Thames Water |
| Receiving watercourse | Groundwater |
| Location | 51.86988748928932, -1.745501696505302 |

| Repeat-offender flag (pipeline) | false |

## Rainfall context

| Gauge | Distance | 0–24h before | 24–48h before | During event |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 253340TP | 1.1 km | 0.01 mm | 0.01 mm | 0.0 mm |
| 251556TP | 9.4 km | 0.0 mm | 0.0 mm | 0.52 mm |
| **Maximum** | | **0.01 mm** | **0.01 mm** | **0.52 mm** |

- The only rain recorded during the event (0.52 mm) was at the gauge 9.4 km away.
- No rain radar data for 13–15 November was found to check these gauge readings.

**National context (not local):**
- The Environment Agency's weekly report for 30 Oct–5 Nov 2026, as reported by Water Magazine, said:
  - England remained in drought.
  - About 2 mm of rain fell that week, following a wetter-than-average October (112%).
  - River flows fell at all reporting sites.
  - Groundwater "continued to fall at most monitoring sites" because dry soils limited recharge.
- This report predates the event by about 10 days and gives no local readings. [Water Magazine, 9 Nov 2026](https://www.watermagazine.co.uk/2026/11/09/drought-continues-to-grip-england-as-reservoir-levels-remain-below-average/)

---

## Innocent explanations considered

The skeptic agent rated these possible non-breach explanations:

| Explanation | Skeptic plausibility | Status after evidence review |
|---|---|---|
| High groundwater or infiltration driving the spill | **High** | **Weakened, not eliminated.** National groundwater was falling in early November, but Bourton is a recognised groundwater-impacted network and October was wetter than average. There is no local borehole data. The probable permit does not list groundwater as an allowed cause. |
| Localised rain missed by the nearest gauge | Medium | Largely refuted. The nearest gauge recorded 0.0 mm, and the 0.52 mm at 9.4 km is very small. |
| Pump failure, blockage or power outage | Medium | **Not ruled out.** No reports were found online. If it happened, it would be an operational incident, not a rain-driven spill. |
| Data feed or timestamp error | Medium | Unverified. |
| Sensor fault or glitch | Low | Low weight, since the monitor was online. Unverified. |
| Snowmelt | Low | No support in the data or sources. |
| Tidal influence | Low | Not relevant: the site is inland. |

**Skeptic's strongest objection, stated honestly:**
- The skeptic's own "strongest objection" in fact **supports** a breach: "The discharge persisted for at least 5.6 hours while rainfall measured at the nearest gauge was effectively zero … indicating a probable breach." The skeptic gave a breach confidence of 0.78.
- The strongest **innocent** explanation the skeptic raised was groundwater infiltration (rated high plausibility). This remains the main open question about what physically caused the spill.

**Other open points noted by the adjudicator:**
- The site's identity is unconfirmed, so the permit wording may not apply.
- The "anticipated unavoidable discharges" section of Thames Water's groundwater plan has not been read and may cover events like this.

---

## Web evidence (cited)

1. **Thames Water, Bourton-on-the-Water Groundwater Impacted System Management Plan (hosted by the parish council).** [PDF](https://www.bourtononthewater-pc.gov.uk/wp-content/uploads/sites/114/2025/07/bourton-on-the-water-groundwater-infiltration-mana_250713_233038.pdf)
   - Describes "a permitted land treatment area and overflow to the River Windrush" south of the village, with excess flow carried about 800 m to the land treatment area. A land treatment area may explain the "Groundwater" label.
   - The plan does **not** mention the ID TWL00049.
   - Quotes the permit condition: "The discharge shall only occur when and only for as long as the flow passed forward is equal to or greater than the overflow setting indicated due to rainfall and/or snowmelt."
   - Describes the network: about 41 km of mostly separate foul sewers, serving 4,790 population equivalent.
   - Says the foul system has in recent years been "overwhelmed for weeks or even months at a time" after prolonged heavy rain and raised groundwater.
   - States that "spill to river has occurred on both wet and dry days". No dates or monitoring figures are given.
   - Contains a section on "anticipated unavoidable discharges", not yet reviewed.

2. **Bourton-on-the-Water Parish Council, Emergency Planning page.** Confirms Thames Water produced a groundwater infiltration management plan for Bourton. [Link](https://www.bourtononthewater-pc.gov.uk/the-council/emergency-planning/)

3. **Water Magazine, 9 Nov 2026.** National Environment Agency drought summary for 30 Oct–5 Nov, as described under Rainfall context above. [Link](https://www.watermagazine.co.uk/2026/11/09/drought-continues-to-grip-england-as-reservoir-levels-remain-below-average/)

- reports of a pump failure, blockage or power cut at Bourton (Oct–Nov 2026)
- rain radar for the area
- snowmelt
- the event's end time
- whether Thames Water notified the EA
- local borehole or River Windrush levels
- the EA weekly report for 6–12 November

---

## Confidence and recommendation

**Confidence:** moderate to high that this event warrants investigation as a possible breach. Adjudicator confidence is 0.68; skeptic breach confidence is 0.78.

**Supporting a breach:**
- Effectively zero rainfall at 1.1 km before and during the event.
- At least 5.6 hours of discharge with the monitor online.
- The probable permit allows spills only for rainfall or snowmelt.
- Thames Water's own plan acknowledges past dry-day spills.
- National groundwater was falling in early November.

**Limiting confidence:**
- The site has not been confirmed as the Bourton overflow.
- There is no local groundwater data for 15 November.
- An operational fault has not been excluded.
- The "unavoidable discharges" section of the plan has not been reviewed.

**Recommendation:** send to the Environment Agency as a **possible** breach for investigation. Before sending, the reviewer may wish to:
- check TWL00049 against Thames Water's monitoring or permit register to confirm whether it is the Bourton land-treatment overflow
- read the "anticipated unavoidable discharges" section of the plan

It quotes the permit condition as allowing discharge only "due to rainfall and/or snowmelt". The plan also states that spills have occurred "on both wet and dry days".

> - Bourton is a recognised groundwater-impacted network, so groundwater infiltration may have contributed. However, national EA reporting for 30 Oct–5 Nov 2026 showed groundwater falling at most sites.

evidence.report:
I couldn't find any public report of this overflow event, a pump failure or a sewage sighting. The press I did find says Saturday 14 November was dry, and the gauge data shows no rain in the 48 hours before the spill. That keeps the case for a dry-weather spill **moderately strong but unconfirmed**. One thing slightly weakens it: Met Office forecasts reported in the press predicted heavy rain on 10–11 November, 3–4 days before the spill, which the 48-hour gauge window doesn't cover.

**What I searched (5 searches, 3 pages read in full)**

1. **Roding sewage news for November 2026:** nothing about this river or event, just general Thames Water stories and content-farm pages, which I left out.
2. **Local weather on 14 November:** nothing for Redbridge or Woodford. The results were about the US, South Africa and Waltham, Massachusetts, so I left them out.
3. **Pump failures or power cuts:** the only result was a Thames Water *drinking-water* supply failure from 10 November at the Lower Hall booster station in Chingford, affecting areas such as E4 and EN postcodes. It came only through syndicated "999" aggregator sites, it involves the supply network rather than the sewers, and Redbridge wasn't listed. So it's no evidence of a sewer pump failure here, and I don't rely on it.
4. **London rain in early November:** found useful forecast articles (below).
5. **Overflows, permits and investigations on the Roding:** found background only, nothing about this overflow ID (TWL00794).

**Supports a breach**
- **The night of the spill was dry.** A Met Office-based report published on Sunday 15 November describes "a largely dry and sunny Saturday" (14 November) in London, with highs of about 9°C. That matches all three gauges reading about 0 mm. https://uk.news.yahoo.com/london-faces-wet-sunday-heavy-050000591.html
- **The next day's rain came after the spill ended.** The same article forecast rain arriving on the Sunday *morning*, with a 70% chance by 8am. The spill ended at 02:26 UTC, so this rain can't explain it (same URL).
- **The days before were forecast dry.** Thursday 12 November was expected to be "mostly dry" with possibly an isolated shower, and Friday 13 November "largely dry" with sunshine. That fits the gauges' near-zero 24–48h reading. https://www.london-now.co.uk/news/26710683.london-weather-week---met-office-forecasts-heavy-rain/
- **Background on the Roding (not about this event):** a government answer to Parliament (February 2025) says the river faces "storm overflow discharges… misconnections, and pollution incidents". It also mentions a Thames Water study of options to reduce spills at the Snakes Lane overflow. https://questions-statements.parliament.uk/written-questions/detail/2025-01-27/26705/ I haven't confirmed whether TWL00794 is the Snakes Lane overflow.

**Supports an innocent explanation**
- **Rain earlier in the week (the skeptic's delayed-response point).** The Met Office forecast rain spreading across London on Tuesday 10 November, "heavy at times" and continuing overnight, with more rain early on Wednesday 11 November (London Now URL above). That falls outside the 48-hour gauge window. Two caveats: this is a *forecast*, not measured rainfall, and it ended about 3 days before the spill. Rain that long ago seems unlikely to cause a 3.6-hour discharge late at night, but it can't be ruled out.
- I found **no** evidence for the other innocent explanations: no sewer pump failure, power cut, blockage, telemetry fault, snowmelt or tidal effect. Snowmelt looks very unlikely given highs of about 9–10°C.

**Still unknown**
- Whether Thames Water's own spill data shows this event, and what cause it gave.
- The overflow's name, permit number and minimum flow it must pass on to treatment, and whether the treatment works was meeting it.
- Whether this site is under Environment Agency investigation or enforcement.
- What the null status field means.
- Radar rainfall, and actual measured rain on 10–11 November in the Roding catchment.
- Any water-quality readings or sightings of pollution downstream.
- Which site is the company's existing "likely breach" case.

**Overall:** the dry weather on 14–15 November is confirmed by press reports as well as the gauges. Only the possible delayed effect of the 10–11 November rain and a still-untested monitor fault stand against a breach. The skeptic's 0.78 breach confidence looks reasonable. Getting Thames Water's spill log for this event, plus measured rainfall for 10–11 November, would settle most of what's left.

searches.answer:
The information provided describes concerns about both permitted and unpermitted Thames Water discharges into the River Roding, including around Redbridge and South Woodford, but it does not establish the findings or outcome of a specific Environment Agency permit investigation.

Relevant details:
- Thames21 said the River Roding was among the areas badly affected by storm-overflow discharges and called for investigation, monitoring and remedial action.
- Redbridge Council called on Thames Water to address discharges in the Roding and its tributaries. Its motion cited unsafe bacteria levels and a particularly severe contamination finding linked to an **unpermitted discharge into Alders Brook**.

report:
# Evidence pack: possible dry-weather spill, Thames Water overflow TWL00794 (River Roding)

**Pipeline verdict:** likely_breach. **Adjudicated confidence:** 0.77.

---

## Summary

Thames Water storm overflow **TWL00794** recorded a discharge to the **River Roding** lasting **3.6 hours**, from **14 Nov 2026 22:48** to **15 Nov 2026 02:26 UTC** (GMT, so UTC is local time).

- **Rain gauges:** all three nearby Environment Agency (EA) gauges recorded effectively no rain during the spill or in the 48 hours before it. The nearest gauge is 1.1 km away.
- **Press reports:** a Met Office-based report describes Saturday 14 November in London as "largely dry and sunny". The next rain was forecast for after the spill ended.
- **Monitor:** the monitor was online.

The main innocent explanation still standing is a **delayed catchment or groundwater response** to heavy rain **forecast** for 10–11 November. That rain fell outside the gauge window and has not been confirmed by measurement. A monitor fault and an operational emergency have not been tested.

This is a **possible** breach that merits investigation, not a confirmed one.

---

## The spill (data)

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Overflow ID | TWL00794 |
| Company | Thames Water |
| Receiving watercourse | River Roding |
| Location | 51.58477, 0.03955 |
| Event start | 2026-11-14 22:48 UTC |
| Event end | 2026-11-15 02:26 UTC |
| Duration | 3.6 h |
| Monitor offline | false |
| Status field | **null** (meaning unknown) |
| Feed classification | dry_spill_candidate |

Source: spill monitoring feed record for TWL00794.

---

## Rainfall context

EA rain gauge readings (mm):

| Gauge | Distance | 24–48 h before | 0–24 h before | During spill |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 239374TP | 1.1 km | 0.0 | 0.0 | 0.0 |
| 239579TP | 7.1 km | 0.04 | 0.0 | 0.0 |
| 540001RG | 7.1 km | 0.03 | 0.03 | 0.0 |
| **Max** | | **0.04** | **0.03** | **0.0** |

Press reports on the weather (London-wide, not specific to the catchment):

- **14 Nov:** described as "a largely dry and sunny Saturday", with highs of about 9°C. [Yahoo News UK, 15 Nov](https://uk.news.yahoo.com/london-faces-wet-sunday-heavy-050000591.html)
- **15 Nov:** rain was forecast from Sunday morning, after the spill had ended at 02:26. [Yahoo News UK](https://uk.news.yahoo.com/london-faces-wet-sunday-heavy-050000591.html)
- **12–13 Nov:** forecast "mostly dry" (possibly an isolated shower) and "largely dry". [London Now](https://www.london-now.co.uk/news/26710683.london-weather-week---met-office-forecasts-heavy-rain/)
- **10–11 Nov:** Met Office forecast rain "heavy at times" on Tuesday 10 November, continuing overnight into early Wednesday 11 November. This falls **outside** the 48-hour gauge window and is a **forecast, not a measurement**. [London Now](https://www.london-now.co.uk/news/26710683.london-weather-week---met-office-forecasts-heavy-rain/)

**Limitation:** the gauge data covers only the 48 hours before the spill. No radar data or measured rainfall for 10–11 November has been obtained.

---

## Innocent explanations considered

| Explanation | Status | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Unrecorded local downpour | Refuted | All three gauges read 0.0 mm during the spill; the press describes the day as dry |
| Rain from the following day | Refuted | Sunday rain was forecast after the 02:26 end |
| Snowmelt or thaw | Refuted | Highs of about 9–10°C; no snow reported |
| **Delayed or groundwater response to 10–11 Nov rain** | **Standing** | Forecast heavy rain about 3 days earlier. Weakened because it is unmeasured and the gap is long, but infiltration-prone catchments can respond late |
| Monitor or telemetry false positive | Standing (untested) | Monitor online; no fault reported, but none ruled out |
| Pump failure, power loss or other emergency | Standing (unverified) | No evidence found for the sewer network |
| Tidal back-pressure | Standing (speculative) | The lower Roding is tidal near Barking; nothing in the data supports this |
| Data or timestamp processing error | Standing (low) | Speculative |

**The skeptic's strongest objection, stated honestly:** the skeptic's own summary argued *for* a breach. It said the online monitor, the 3.6-hour duration and the near-zero rain across all gauges make a glitch or missed rain "far less likely", and put breach confidence at 0.78.

The strongest *innocent* case the skeptic raised, and the one that survives adjudication, is **groundwater infiltration or delayed runoff from rain more than 48 hours earlier**. The press forecasts for 10–11 November give this some support, but the rain has not been measured.

---

## Web evidence (cited)

1. **Weather on 14–15 November:** [Yahoo News UK, "London faces wet Sunday…"](https://uk.news.yahoo.com/london-faces-wet-sunday-heavy-050000591.html). It describes 14 November as largely dry and sunny, with rain forecast later on 15 November.
2. **Weather on 10–13 November:** [London Now, "London weather this week – Met Office forecasts heavy rain"](https://www.london-now.co.uk/news/26710683.london-weather-week---met-office-forecasts-heavy-rain/). It gives heavy rain forecast for 10–11 November and mostly dry conditions for 12–13 November.
3. **Background on the Roding (not about this event):** [UK Parliament written answer 26705 (Feb 2025)](https://questions-statements.parliament.uk/written-questions/detail/2025-01-27/26705/). It says the Roding faces storm overflow discharges, misconnections and pollution incidents. It also mentions a Thames Water study of options to reduce spills at the Snakes Lane combined sewer overflow. **It is not confirmed that TWL00794 is Snakes Lane.**

Searches found **no** public report of:
- this event,
- a sewer pump failure or power cut, or
- sewage sightings on the Roding for these dates.

---

## Confidence and recommendation

**Confidence: 0.77 (likely breach, unconfirmed).**

**Recommendation:** refer to the EA as a possible dry-weather discharge for investigation. The key gaps are:

1. Thames Water's own EDM/spill log for this event and the cause it recorded.
2. Measured and radar rainfall for the Roding catchment, especially 10–11 November.
3. Overflow name, permit number and pass-forward flow condition, and whether the downstream works was treating its required flow.
4. Any operational incidents, sensor faults or maintenance on the serving network on 14–15 November.
5. The meaning of the null status field.
6. Downstream water quality readings (ammonia, dissolved oxygen) around 14–15 November.

---

## Draft message to the Environment Agency

> **Subject:** Report of a POSSIBLE storm overflow permit breach for investigation: Thames Water TWL00794, River Roding, 14–15 Nov 2026
>
> Dear Environment Agency,
>
> I am writing to report a **possible** breach of storm overflow permit conditions and to ask that you investigate it. This is not a confirmed breach.
>
> **Event:** Thames Water overflow TWL00794 (approx. 51.5848, 0.0395) recorded a discharge to the River Roding from 22:48 on 14 November 2026 to 02:26 on 15 November 2026 (3.6 hours). The monitor was reported online.
>
> **Why it may be a dry-weather spill:**
> - Your rain gauges 239374TP (1.1 km), 239579TP (7.1 km) and 540001RG (7.1 km) recorded 0.0 mm during the discharge, at most 0.03 mm in the preceding 24 hours and at most 0.04 mm in the 24–48 hours before.
> - Press reporting of the Met Office forecast describes 14 November in London as largely dry and sunny. Rain was forecast for after the discharge ended.
>
> **Caveats:**
> - Heavy rain was forecast for London on 10–11 November, about three days earlier. A delayed or groundwater-related response cannot be excluded.
> - I have not been able to rule out a monitor fault or an operational incident.
> - The site's status field in the published data is blank.
>
> **I would be grateful if you could check:**
> - Thames Water's EDM record and stated cause for this event.
> - Measured rainfall in the catchment for 10–11 November.
> - The permit conditions and pass-forward flow compliance at the time.
> - Any reported operational incidents on 14–15 November.
>
> **Sources:**
> - https://uk.news.yahoo.com/london-faces-wet-sunday-heavy-050000591.html
> - https://www.london-now.co.uk/news/26710683.london-weather-week---met-office-forecasts-heavy-rain/
>
> Yours faithfully,
> [Name, contact details]
